ECMA-262 10.1.8.1 OrdinaryGet returns `undefined` for a property the object does not have, so for an instantiation consistent with this local site - any caller passing a `number[]` shorter than two elements - the value of `s[1]` is `undefined`. Under the frozen recipe TypeScript types that expression `number`, so the static type does NOT mark the optionality, and the local site contains no optionality marker, unwrap operator, default-supplying operator or presence test. Condition 3 (no local signal) and condition 4 (LED fails: the local site plus the reference do not fix a single outcome) both hold. complexity_detail.description: Object values are references: assignment and argument passing copy the reference, never the object, with nothing written for the sharing.
Array type `T[]`: an Array exotic object whose `length` is maintained automatically, which is what makes it the growable sequence type.
complexity_detail.citation: TypeScript Handbook (TypeScript 7.0.2, the frozen toolchain version) 'Everyday Types / Arrays'; ECMA-262 (ECMAScript 2022, 13th edition) 10.4.2 'Array Exotic Objects'

complexity_detail.description: Array literal `[e, ...]` creates a new Array object with own data properties for the elements.
Index / member access `a[e]`: the key expression is converted by ToPropertyKey and the object's [[Get]] is invoked.
Absent-property rule: an index for which no own or inherited property exists evaluates to `undefined`, with no failure and nothing written at the site.
The STATIC type of an index access depends on the `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` compiler option rather than on the construct: `T` when it is off and `T | undefined` when it is on.
Arrow function expression `(params) => body`: creates a function object with a lexical `this`.
A concise (expression) arrow body implicitly returns its expression; no `return` is written.
`return expr` completes the enclosing function with that value.
Return-type inference: an unannotated function's return type is inferred from its return expressions.
complexity_detail.citation: TypeScript Handbook (TypeScript 7.0.2, the frozen toolchain version) 'More on Functions / Return Type Annotations'

hidden_items.why: Local site 2, `const [q, r] = divmod2(7, 3)`. The binding pattern is specified as a call to GetIterator (ECMA-262 8.5.2), which performs a dynamic property lookup of `@@iterator` along the value's prototype chain; that property is writable and configurable, so two or more distinct bodies can execute for this local form. The candidate-equivalence exclusion is not established on the record (it is universal in scope, methodology 04 section 1.4.0, and neither route is available), and no local token fixes the target. Verified by execution: witnesses/F06.P2/typescript/w_iter.ts.

hidden_items.checklist_item: H4 - Implicit allocation, copy, move, destruction, or cleanup
hidden_items.why: Local site 2. The destructuring creates an Array Iterator object (ECMA-262 23.1.3.36 CreateArrayIterator) on every execution. `const [q, r]` is a BINDING PATTERN, not a composite literal, a constructor call or a `new`-style operator, so H4's 'allocation named by a local token' exclusion does not apply: nothing written at the site names an allocation. The allocation of the tuple ITSELF, at local site 1, is excluded - an array literal is a composite literal - and is not counted.

Local site 3, `return q + r`. The types of `q` and `r` are established at local site 2, which methodology 04 section 0.7 expressly excludes from what is local to site 3. ECMAScript `+` applies ToPrimitive to both operands and then, if either result is a String, converts the OTHER to a String and concatenates (ECMA-262 13.15.3 ApplyStringOrNumericBinaryOperator). The inserted conversion changes the value, the representation and the operation performed, it is written nowhere at the site, and the LED gate fails because the local site plus the reference admit both numeric addition and string concatenation. Observed: witnesses/F07.P1/typescript/w_arith.ts prints `any string coercion: 6!`, where `+` concatenated instead of adding.

hidden_items.why: Local site 3, `return q + r` - a DIFFERENT local site and a DIFFERENT registry rule from the H3 event above, so a distinct event under methodology 04 section 1.3.2. ECMA-262 7.1.1 ToPrimitive looks up `@@toPrimitive` and then OrdinaryToPrimitive calls `valueOf` and `toString` from the operand's prototype chain, so arbitrary user bodies can execute at this operator. Observed: w_arith.ts prints `any user valueOf: 7 global written: true`, showing user code running - and writing a global - at a bare `*`/`+`.

Local site 3, `return q + r`, sub-test H8b. The numeric types this local form admits are Number and BigInt, and the reference does NOT give one and the same documented outcome across the edge classes the form can reach: Number::add overflows to Infinity and rounds (ECMA-262 6.1.6.1.7) while BigInt::add is exact and has no overflow edge (6.1.6.2), and mixing the two throws a TypeError (13.15.3). No local token selects the edge behaviour. The third exclusion bullet does not rescue it: the variation does arise from the operands' declared types, but there is no SINGLE UNIFORM RULE PER EDGE CLASS across those types, which that bullet also requires. Note for contrast that H8 does NOT fire at local site 1, where the operand types `a: number, b: number` are written inside the same local site and ECMA-262 6.1.6.1.5/6.1.6.1.6 then fix exactly one outcome for every edge class, independent of mode and target.

The assignment-target exclusion does not apply: `xs` is not an assignment target here. The LED gate fails because the reference does not fix one outcome from the local site alone - the receiver's declaration, which decides whether `sort` is the built-in or a user method, is elsewhere. Nothing at the site is a composite literal, a constructor call, a `new`-style operator or an explicit allocation call for that List, so H4's 'allocation named by a local token' exclusion does not apply. The comparator's OWN function object, by contrast, IS named by the arrow written at the site and is excluded, not counted.

facts.justification: ECMA-262 (ECMAScript 2022, 13th edition) 6.1 lists Number among the primitive types and 6.1.6.1.7 creates no object. TypeScript performs no boxing at an arithmetic operator - contrast a language that boxes a primitive when it crosses a generic boundary.

determinacy_enumeration: CLASS 1 - both operands are Numbers (the probe's declared domain as TypeScript can express it): IEEE-754 binary64 addition with NO conversion applied to either operand. In-scope axes per Rule 1.4.1 (A5 conversion_behavior, A4 type_and_representation, A10 overflow_exceptional_numeric, A1 value_vs_storage): A5 = none, A4 = binary floating point, A10 = rounding / NaN / Inf, A1 = copy. WITNESS: the frozen probe file, built and run under the frozen recipe, printing 3.5; witnesses/F10.P2/typescript/w_sum.ts prints `num+num: 3.5 | 0.1+0.2: 0.30000000000000004 | overflow: Infinity`.

CLASS 2 - both operands are BigInts: exact arbitrary-precision addition with no conversion and NO OVERFLOW EDGE AT ALL (A4 = arbitrary-precision integer, A10 = mathematically exact). Materially different from class 1 on dimensions 8 (representation) and 9 (observable result): the same two tokens compute a value class 1 would round away. ECMA-262 6.1.6.2.7 'BigInt::add'. WITNESS: w_sum.ts prints `bigint: 1180591620717411303425n`.

CLASS 3 - at least one operand is a String: `+` is not arithmetic at all but STRING CONCATENATION, with the other operand converted to a String and a new String allocated (A5 = textual coercion, A4 = text, A10 not applicable). Materially different on dimensions 4, 6, 8 and 9. ECMA-262 13.15.3, the 'If lprim is a String or rprim is a String' step. WITNESS: w_sum.ts prints `string: ab1 string` - the result's `typeof` is `string`.

CLASS 4 - at least one operand is an object: ECMA-262 7.1.1 ToPrimitive runs a user-definable `@@toPrimitive`, `valueOf` or `toString` at the operator, which may allocate, mutate non-local state, throw, or produce a primitive of any of the classes above (A5 = user-defined conversion, A4 = user-defined type). Rule 1.4.7 counts this because it makes classes reachable the built-in operator cannot reach, not merely because the target varies. WITNESS: w_sum.ts prints `object valueOf: 5 side effect: true` - the user body ran and wrote a global at a bare `+`. EXCLUDED CLASSES, with citation and refutation witness as Rule 1.3.1.e requires. (a) A5 = LOSSLESS WIDENING - NOT REALIZABLE, flagged LOW-B-BY-ABSENCE, and it is the class this probe exists to find: TypeScript has no integer type to widen from, so no completion of this fragment performs an integer-to-float promotion. Refutation witness: w_sum.ts's `num+num` line, where two operands the probe calls 'an integer' and 'a double' are the same type and neither changes representation; and the mixed Number/BigInt completion, which does NOT widen but instead THROWS - `THREW: Cannot mix BigInt and other types, use explicit conversions` - so the language's two numeric types never promote into one another. (b) A5 = sign reinterpretation, boxing/unboxing/existential wrapping - NOT REALIZABLE: ECMAScript has no unsigned numeric type and performs no boxing at an arithmetic operator. (c) A10 = wraps modulo 2**n / saturates / traps / undefined on overflow / build-mode dependent - NOT REALIZABLE: 6.1.6.1.7 is IEEE-754 with a defined Infinity result, identical under every entry the frozen recipe lists. (d) A1 = alias to the operand's own storage, move, or deferred evaluation - NOT REALIZABLE: the operands are read by GetValue and ECMAScript has no by-reference operand form and no lazy operand form. Note on the completions used as witnesses below: methodology 03 Rule 1.3.1 requires a witness to be a concrete completion of the probe program outside the measured fragment, built and run under the frozen recipe. `--strict` turns on `noImplicitAny`, which forbids an INFERRED `any`; it does not forbid an explicitly written `any`, and the TypeScript Handbook documents `any` as a first-class type ('Everyday Types / any'). Completions that declare the given operands `any`, `bigint` or `string` therefore build and run under the frozen recipe unmodified, which is what makes the classes below realizable rather than hypothetical. Each was executed.

conversion_behavior: ECMA-262 13.15.3 branches on whether EITHER operand's primitive is a String, so the left declaration alone does not settle whether the operator adds or concatenates. Two variables are two declared entities (Rule 2.2.2). |G| = 0: no fact in this probe's frozen semantic_facts_expected set is decided by a compiler mode or target; ECMA-262 6.1.6.1 fixes binary64 and its arithmetic identically under every entry the frozen recipe lists. Note also what does NOT cost a hop here: once the two declarations are read, no further consultation is needed for conversion_behavior, because the language's answer - no conversion between two Numbers - is fixed by the specification (Rule 2.2.3 zero-cost knowledge), whereas a language with several integer widths would need the promotion table as well.

hidden_items.why: The fragment's single local site, `const sum = i + d`. ECMA-262 13.15.3 inserts ToPrimitive and then either ToString (concatenation) or ToNumeric (arithmetic) on BOTH operands, with nothing written at the site, and the inserted conversion changes the value, the representation, the result type and the operation performed. The operand declarations are at a different local site (methodology 04 section 0.7), so the LED gate fails. OBSERVED: `string: ab1 string`.

hidden_items.why: Same local site, a different registry rule. ECMA-262 7.1.1 ToPrimitive looks up `@@toPrimitive` and then OrdinaryToPrimitive calls `valueOf` and `toString` from the operand's prototype chain, so two or more distinct bodies can execute at a bare `+`. The per-candidate equivalence exclusion is universal in scope (methodology 04 section 1.4.0) and is not established on the record. OBSERVED: `object valueOf: 5 side effect: true`.

hidden_items.checklist_item: H4 - Implicit allocation, copy, move, destruction, or cleanup
hidden_items.why: Same local site, a third rule. When either operand's primitive is a String, ECMA-262 13.15.3 produces a NEW String by concatenation, which is an allocation the form performs with nothing written for it - no composite literal, no constructor, no `new`, no explicit allocation call - so H4's 'allocation named by a local token' exclusion does not apply. OBSERVED: `string: ab1 string`. When both operands are Numbers no allocation occurs at all, which is why this event exists only because the operand types are not written at the site.

Same local site, sub-test H8b. The numeric types this local form admits are Number and BigInt, and the reference does not give one and the same documented outcome across the edge classes the form can reach: Number::add rounds and saturates to Infinity (ECMA-262 6.1.6.1.7) while BigInt::add is exact with no overflow edge (6.1.6.2.7), and mixing the two throws (13.15.3). No local token selects the edge behaviour, and the 'variation arises only from the declared operand types' exclusion additionally requires a SINGLE UNIFORM RULE PER EDGE CLASS across the admitted types, which does not hold. H8a does NOT fire: ECMAScript's numeric semantics are identical under every build mode and target the frozen recipe admits, which is a genuine TypeScript result and the reason locality records |G| = 0.

complexity_detail.description: ToPrimitive and then ToNumeric (or ToString) are applied to both operands of `+` with nothing written for it.
`+` is the exception among the arithmetic operators: a String primitive on either side makes it STRING CONCATENATION, allocating a new String, rather than addition.
Mixing a BigInt operand with a non-BigInt operand throws a TypeError instead of converting - the one place the language refuses a numeric conversion rather than performing it silently.
